# Incident Report — Malware-Traffic-Analysis Exercise 2024-07-30

**Evidence source:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 packets, 585.7 sec, capture window 2024-07-30 06:38:48 UTC – 06:48:34 UTC). No separate IDS/alert export was present in the evidence folder; findings below are derived directly from packet analysis with `tshark`.

## 1. Infected Host

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **172.16.1.66** | Consistent source IP across all traffic below |
| MAC address | **00:1e:64:ec:f3:08** | ARP replies and Ethernet frames to/from 172.16.1.66 |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** (AD domain `wiresharkworkshop.online`, DC = WIRESHARK-WS-DC / 172.16.1.4) | NBNS name registration for 172.16.1.66; Kerberos `CNameString` = `DESKTOP-SKBR25F$`; also self-identified in the malware C2 beacon (see below) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **ccollier** | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ `CNameString` = `ccollier` between 172.16.1.66 ↔ 172.16.1.4; also self-reported in every C2 beacon |
| OS (as reported by host) | Microsoft Windows 11 Pro, 64-bit | Verbatim field in the malware's own C2 beacon string |

## 2. Malware Family

**STRRAT** — a Java-based remote access trojan.

**Attribution: signature-confirmed, not behavioral.** The malware's own command-and-control protocol is unencrypted, pipe-delimited plaintext and literally names itself in every beacon (TCP stream 172.16.1.66:49754 → 141.98.10.79:12132, first seen at capture time +76.99s, frame 9117 onward):

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender||1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|1 Sec
```

Field breakdown: `ping` (beacon type) | `STRRAT` (family name) | `1BE8292C` (campaign/build ID — not a file hash, only 8 hex chars) | hostname | logged-in user | OS | architecture | installed AV (Windows Defender) | client version `1.6` | victim country | installer-lock status | uptime counter.

This beacon repeats at a steady **~5-second interval** for the remainder of the capture (last beacon observed at +585.66s, reporting "5 min 10 sec" uptime), confirming a live, persistent C2 channel rather than a one-off connection. Several beacons carry a 9th field that is base64-encoded and decodes to the victim's **active foreground window title** (e.g. `RG9jdW1lbnRz`→"Documents", `SG9tZQ==`→"Home", `UGljdHVyZXM=`→"Pictures", `UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy`→"Program Manager", `RmFuYWQgSGVhZCBMaWdodGhvdXNlIC0gUGFpbnQ=`→"Fanad Head Lighthouse - Paint"), confirming active screen/window-activity surveillance capability consistent with STRRAT.

No response payload larger than a TCP ACK was ever sent by the C2 server in this capture — only the client-side heartbeat/telemetry was observed; no interactive command traffic captured.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

### Command-and-control
- **141.98.10.79:12132** — raw TCP (no TLS), cleartext STRRAT beacon protocol as shown above. This is the confirmed C2 endpoint.

### Malicious/abused domains and URLs (delivery chain, immediately preceding first C2 beacon)
- `github.com` (140.82.113.3) — TLS connection at capture time +64.05s (small, ~5 KB, page/redirect-sized)
- `objects.githubusercontent.com` (185.199.110.133) — TLS connection at +64.83s, 833 KB transferred; GitHub's raw-content CDN, consistent with hosting the actual payload/dropper file (contents not recoverable — HTTPS)
- `repo1.maven.org` (199.232.196.209) — three parallel TLS sessions starting at +68.00s, totaling **~13.9 MB** downloaded (4.51 MB + 2.80 MB + 1.58 MB). This volume/pattern is consistent with a Java RAT pulling its runtime dependency JARs from Maven Central after initial execution.
- `http://ip-api.com/json/` (208.95.112.1) — plaintext HTTP GET at +567.86s (relative offset within capture; frame 9111). Response confirms the malware performed victim geolocation/IP fingerprinting: public IP `136.49.34.127`, geolocated to Austin, Texas, US. `ip-api.com` is a legitimate service being abused here as a recon step by the malware, not itself malicious infrastructure.
- `javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com` (23.194.164.136) — legitimate Oracle Java auto-update check; its presence confirms a Java Runtime Environment is installed/active on the host, which STRRAT (a JAR-based RAT) requires to execute.

**Timeline:** github.com browse (+64.05s) → objects.githubusercontent.com payload fetch (+64.83s) → repo1.maven.org dependency downloads (+68.00s to ~+73.8s) → first STRRAT C2 beacon to 141.98.10.79:12132 (+76.99s). This sequence is the observed infection chain.

### Transferred files / hashes
No cleartext file transfer of the actual malware binary/JAR was observed — the GitHub and Maven downloads occurred entirely over HTTPS/TLS, so no filename or SHA256 hash of the payload can be extracted from this packet capture. The only cleartext HTTP file objects in the capture are benign: `http://www.msftconnecttest.com/connecttest.txt` (Microsoft connectivity test, plain text "Microsoft Connect Test") and the `ip-api.com` JSON geolocation response. The only file-like identifier recoverable from the traffic is the STRRAT **campaign/build ID `1BE8292C`**, which is a malware-internal tag, not a cryptographic hash.

### Non-indicators (ruled out)
All other traffic (LDAP/CLDAP/Kerberos/DRSUAPI/SMB2/RPC to 172.16.1.4, and TLS sessions to Microsoft/MSN/Bing/Skype/Office/Windows telemetry endpoints) is standard Active Directory domain-member and Windows/Office background traffic, and does not indicate lateral movement or a secondary C2 channel — only one non-standard destination port (141.98.10.79:12132) exists in the entire capture.

## Summary
Host **DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66, MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08)**, logged in as domain user **ccollier**, is infected with **STRRAT** (Java RAT), signature-confirmed via its self-identifying plaintext C2 protocol. The malware beacons every ~5 seconds to **141.98.10.79:12132**, exfiltrates host fingerprint and active-window titles, and its delivery chain traces through **github.com / objects.githubusercontent.com** (payload) and **repo1.maven.org** (Java dependency retrieval) immediately before C2 activation. Recommend isolating the host, blocking 141.98.10.79/32 at the perimeter, and resetting the ccollier account credentials.
